regions.name: Northeast
regions.climate: Humid continental (Köppen Dfa/Dfb), humid subtropical along the southern coast; cold winters with snow cover inland, warm humid summers.
regions.summary: Four distinct seasons with precipitation spread evenly through the year. Winter cold, freeze–thaw cycles, road salt and deer browse shape plant choice more than summer drought does.
designGuidance: Plan for winter: evergreen structure, persistent fruit, bark and grass seedheads carry the garden for four to five months.
Keep salt-sensitive plants (white pine, sugar maple, boxwood) out of plow and road-spray zones; use salt-tolerant species along drives and walks.
Deer pressure is high in most suburbs; favour high deer-resistance plants near woods edges or budget for fencing.
Plant in spring after soils drain, or late summer to early fall so roots establish before the ground freezes.
Heavy wet snow splits multi-leader shrubs and arborvitae; keep them clear of roof drip lines.
Many common landscape shrubs (Japanese barberry, burning bush, Norway maple) are regulated or banned in several Northeast states — check the state list before specifying.

regions.name: Southeast
regions.climate: Humid subtropical (Köppen Cfa); long hot humid summers, mild short winters, frequent summer thunderstorms and tropical-storm season June–November.
regions.summary: A long growing season with abundant but uneven rainfall, heavy clay in the Piedmont and fast-draining sands on the Coastal Plain. Heat, humidity and disease pressure matter more than winter cold. Covers north and central Florida; south Florida (zones 10b–11) is out of the pilot.
designGuidance: Fall through early winter is the best planting season: roots grow in warm soil while top growth is dormant and evaporation is low.
Choose plants for humid heat as well as cold hardiness; many northern perennials and conifers fail from summer heat and disease, not winter.
Amend compacted Piedmont clay over whole beds rather than individual holes, and plant slightly high so crowns drain.
Use wind-firm, deep-rooted trees (live oak, bald cypress, sabal palm) where hurricanes and tropical storms are expected, and keep large trees away from houses.
Several popular ornamentals (nandina, lantana, Mexican petunia, Chinese wisteria) are listed invasive in Florida; native alternatives exist for each.
Pine straw is the regional mulch; keep it 5–8 cm deep and away from siding where termites are a concern.

regions.name: Southwest
regions.climate: Hot desert and semi-arid (Köppen BWh/BSk); very hot summers, mild winters at low elevation, bimodal rain from winter storms and the July–September monsoon. Higher plateaus are much colder.
regions.summary: Defaults represent the low and middle Sonoran Desert (around Tucson); Phoenix and Las Vegas are hotter and drier, and Albuquerque, Flagstaff and Santa Fe are several zones colder — set the site zone and frost dates accordingly. Water, heat, alkaline soils and sun intensity drive plant choice.
designGuidance: Plant in fall (October–November) or late winter; avoid May–June, when heat and dry winds stress new roots.
Group plants into hydrozones on separate irrigation valves; water deeply and infrequently to build deep roots, and plan to taper irrigation once desert-adapted plants establish.
Use inorganic mulch (decomposed granite, gravel) around cacti and succulents; reserve organic mulch for shade trees and moister beds.
Give western and southern exposures heat-tolerant plants and use deciduous trees to shade walls and paving in summer while letting winter sun through.
Keep spiny agaves and cacti at least 1 m back from walks, play areas and pool decks.
Saguaro, ocotillo and many other native cacti and trees are protected; buy nursery-grown or permitted salvage plants with tags.
Fountain grass and buffelgrass carry fire into desert plant communities; use native grasses such as deer grass, big sacaton and blue grama instead.
